documents.abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered.

Background: Guideline-based clinical decision support (CDS) tools have become central to promoting evidence-based, high-quality primary care. Despite widespread implementation, clinician adoption and sustained use remain inconsistent. Existing research has typically examined technological usability or organizational implementation factors separately, providing limited understanding of how these influences interact in real-world primary care settings. This study examined how organizational implementation context and clinician technology acceptance jointly shape adoption and sustained use of guideline-based CDS tools in US primary care using an integrated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) perspective. Methods: A qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis was conducted with 13 US primary care clinicians, including physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and pharmacists with prescribing authority. Participants were purposively recruited from diverse ambulatory settings. Semi-structured interviews explored experiences with CDS usability, workflow integration, organizational support, trust, cognitive burden, and implementation processes. Data were analyzed iteratively using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, informed by CFIR and TAM. Results: Six interrelated themes emerged. Clinician acceptance and sustained use of CDS were shaped by (1) workflow integration, (2) organizational legitimacy and leadership support, (3) preservation of clinical judgment, particularly with emerging AI-enabled CDS, (4) social reinforcement and team-based implementation, (5) cognitive and resource constraints, and (6) clinician role, experience, and digital comfort. Across themes, acceptance was driven less by technological capability than by the interaction of workflow design, organizational context, implementation climate, trust, and clinician perceptions. Conclusion: Guideline-based CDS implementation is fundamentally a sociotechnical process requiring alignment between technology, workflow, organizational context, and clinician acceptance. Integrating CFIR and TAM provides a comprehensive framework for understanding these interactions. The findings informed the TRUST framework, which offers practical implementation guidance emphasizing tailored workflow integration, reinforced organizational legitimacy, usability, social reinforcement, and transparent, trustworthy AI-supported CDS to support sustainable implementation in primary care.

Android apps handle sensitive data, often displayed on screens (i.e., Activities), and protecting these activities is vital for ensuring user privacy. Several studies have demonstrated the risk of private data leakage via screen capture and identified malware exploiting this vulnerability. To mitigate such threats, Google introduced FLAG_SECURE, an activity-level security feature that protects an Activity when set by blocking screen capture and restricting display on non-secure devices. Proper usage of this security feature could significantly reduce data leakage risks. However, to the best of our knowledge, its adoption across diverse Android apps has not been systematically studied. In this work, we present a large-scale empirical study of screenshot-based vulnerabilities in Android apps using a systematic static analysis pipeline, ASSA. The pipeline automatically constructs UI models of activities and fragments by leveraging a customized version of Frontmatter, and combines them with a Large Language Model (LLM) to infer runtime context and identify sensitive user data rendered on screens. We apply ASSA to 5,667 popular real-world Android apps and find that 19.8% contain at least one activity that displays sensitive information without screen-capture protection, while 87.2% of apps do not apply FLAG_SECURE to any activity, exposing credentials, financial information, and location data to screenshot attacks. Beyond quantifying prevalence, we analyze FLAG_SECURE usage patterns and establish a taxonomy that captures diverse factors influencing developers’ decisions to adopt or omit screen protection, including intentional privacy protection, intellectual property safeguarding, and unintentional inheritance from base activities. To assess real-world impact, we further conduct in-depth case studies on 200 vulnerable apps and responsibly disclose our findings to the affected vendors, receiving 6 confirmed patches and 20 acknowledgments, including 11 vendors who reported ongoing efforts toward mitigation. These findings indicate that screenshot-based vulnerabilities are not only widespread but also systematically overlooked in practice, highlighting the need for greater awareness and more careful handling of sensitive on-screen information by developers.

Background Patients recovering from lumbar fusion increasingly seek guidance from large language model (LLM) chatbots when their surgeon is unavailable, but the accuracy, completeness, and safety-related content of such responses have not been compared across models for the postoperative period. Objective To compare the accuracy, quality, safety-related content, and readability of responses from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude to frequently asked postoperative lumbar fusion questions, and to identify the question types for which responses are weakest. Methods Thirty questions, compiled by three neurosurgeons and grouped into six clinical categories, were submitted to each model, each with a standardized, patient-oriented prompt requesting warning signs. Ninety anonymized, randomized responses were rated independently by three blinded neurosurgeons for accuracy and four quality subdomains (clarity, completeness, relevance, and patient safety) on 4-point scales. Readability (Flesch–Kincaid, Flesch Reading Ease, and Gunning Fog), word count, and responses meeting an operational screening criterion for potential harm were also assessed. Models were compared with Friedman and Holm-corrected pairwise tests. Results Accuracy was high for all models without significant differences. Quality, clarity, completeness, relevance, and patient safety differed globally, but effect sizes were small (Kendall's W : 0.10–0.21) and, after correction across the six outcome families, only quality and completeness remained significant, with Gemini scoring lower than ChatGPT and Claude. Gemini had the most favorable readability. ChatGPT responses were the shortest (mean 294 vs. 462 and 445 words); length was unrelated to completeness or readability. Two Gemini responses (6.7%) and none from ChatGPT or Claude met a post hoc operational screening criterion for potential harm (a score of ≤2 on accuracy or patient safety from at least one of three raters, without concurrence from the other two); no response was adjudicated as actually harmful. In exploratory question- and category-level analyses, responses tended to be rated highest for standardized questions and lowest for those requiring individualized judgment or interpretation of wound-related symptoms. Conclusion Responses from contemporary LLMs to common postoperative lumbar fusion questions were generally rated as accurate, with small between-model differences and a model-level divergence between readability and completeness. Because safety-related content was explicitly prompted and no patient outcomes were assessed, these findings describe the quality of safety-related information rather than clinical safety. LLMs may support postoperative patient education but should not replace physician guidance, particularly for warning signs and patient-specific recovery decisions.

documents.abstract: Background: Intensive computer use among administrative workers increases exposure to visual ergonomic factors that may contribute to Computer Vision Syndrome (CVS). Workplace illumination, duration of computer use, and length of employment are important factors to consider in preventing occupational visual complaints. Objective: This study aimed to analyze the association between illumination intensity, duration of computer use, length of employment, and CVS complaints among administrative workers at PT. X in Batam City. Methods: A quantitative study with a cross-sectional design was conducted among 31 administrative workers. Workplace illumination intensity was measured using a lux meter, while the duration of computer use and length of employment were obtained from respondent data. CVS complaints were assessed using the Computer Vision Syndrome Questionnaire (CVS-Q). Bivariate associations were analyzed using Fisher's exact test at a significance level of α=0.05. Results: A total of 77.4% of respondents worked under illumination levels below the occupational standard, 38.7% used computers continuously for ≥120 minutes, 61.3% had worked for ≥5 years, and 80.6% experienced CVS. All respondents exposed to illumination below the standard experienced CVS. A statistically significant association was found between workplace illumination and CVS complaints (p<0.001). In contrast, the duration of computer use (p=0.059) and length of employment (p=0.653) were not significantly associated with CVS complaints. Conclusion: Workplace illumination was significantly associated with CVS complaints among administrative workers, whereas the duration of computer use and length of employment showed no statistically significant associations. Improving workplace illumination according to applicable standards and implementing visual ergonomic measures are recommended to prevent CVS among computer-based workers.Keywords: Computer Vision Syndrome; visual ergonomics; illumination; screen time; length of employment

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Low back pain (LBP) is one of the most common musculoskeletal disorders among office workers due to prolonged sitting, continuous computer use, and poor ergonomic posture. Age and length of employment are factors suspected to contribute to LBP complaints because they are associated with degenerative changes in the musculoskeletal system and cumulative exposure to occupational risk factors. Methods: This study employed an analytical observational design with a cross-sectional approach. The study population consisted of all employees of the Department of Culture and Tourism and the Department of Communication and Informatics of Batam City Government who met the study criteria. A total of 86 respondents were selected using proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were analyzed using the Chi-Square test with a significance level of p<0.05. Results: Statistical analysis showed a significant relationship between age and Low Back Pain complaints (p=0.019) and a significant relationship between length of employment and Low Back Pain complaints (p<0.001). Conclusion: There was a significant relationship between age and length of employment and Low back pain complaints among employees of the Department of Culture and Tourism and the Department of Communication and Informatics of Batam City Government Keywords: Age, Length of Employment, Low back pain.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the evidence base for human and organizational factors (HOF) as an approach to managing OSH, critically evaluating its theoretical coherence, its practical distinctiveness, and its field-validated impact on injury reduction. It describes HOF as an eclectic, sociotechnical integrative domain drawing from industrial, occupational, organizational psychology, ergonomics, and sociology, while noting that it lacks unique practical interventions and operates primarily as a knowledge broker rather than a distinct scientific discipline. The chapter highlights HOF&s;s reliance on non-falsifiable, post-hoc interpretive frameworks, and its problematic dismissal of human error as a valid root cause in incident investigations. Drawing on the available field studies across human factors engineering, ergonomics, human performance improvement, and sociological approaches to safety, it provides practitioners with a critical evidence-based appraisal of HOF, concluding that its claimed contributions to OSH exceed what the field-validated evidence currently supports.

documents.abstract: This working paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for evaluating measurable human control of advanced AI agents: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. It separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that simulations and controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. Five pilot reviews, HIC-001 through HIC-005, illustrate control-specific measures including detection-to-containment time, permission comprehension gap, monitor independence, and instruction provenance integrity. An additional qualitative stress test informed framework refinement; it is not independent validation. The Meta case is based on a reported user account, with permission history, causal interpretation, and severity remaining provisional. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. Version 1.0.1 corrects source wording, incorporates the recovered HIC-0 through HIC-5 definitions, and clarifies evidence limitations. Creator: Human in Control Project. License: CC BY 4.0. The main objective of this study is to explore how pre-service teachers retrospectively describe differences between their prior and current perspectives following participation in a Human Library. This research begins with a review of the literature on the definition and characteristics of Human Libraries and proceeds with the creation of one in a university setting. To this end, the study benefited from the collaboration of the Baketik Foundation, which facilitated contact with five individuals willing to share their testimonies on topics related to human rights. The initial sample consisted of 53 pre-service teachers in the Early Childhood Education Bachelor’s programme at the University of the Basque Country (EHU), although ultimately, following a screening process, the sample was reduced to 51. Data were collected using the “I used to think…/Now I think…” reflection exercise, which the pre-service teachers were asked to complete after listening to the testimonies. The narratives were first examined manually by the researchers to identify recurring ideas and potential thematic categories. Microsoft Copilot and ChatGPT were subsequently used to support the identification and consistency checking of the initial category structure, while the final coding was conducted manually by the researchers. Six thematic categories were identified in both sections of the reflection exercise. The descriptive comparison revealed differences in the frequency and elaboration of participants’ narratives, particularly regarding empathy and changes in perspective, peace and social justice, women’s rights and gender-based violence, and silence, social taboos and lack of awareness. Because both sections were produced retrospectively after the Human Library experience, these differences are interpreted as features of participants’ accounts rather than as direct evidence of objectively measured changes in their perspectives.

documents.abstract: Introduction The transition to Industry 5.0 is transforming manufacturing through the integration of smart technologies, while simultaneously increasing the need to protect workers’ health and reduce occupational risks. This systematic review synthesized cross-sectoral evidence on human-centered Industry 5.0 technologies for assessing and reducing occupational risks, with a focus on ergonomic outcomes, worker-related factors, and the conditions influencing their implementation and transferability. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in Scopus and Web of Science following the PRISMA 2020 framework and predefined eligibility criteria based on PECO. Included studies were analyzed according to technology type, occupational risk addressed, ergonomic dimension, assessment method, reported outcomes, implementation conditions, and implications for occupational health and safety, yielding a total of 78 studies that met the inclusion criteria. Results The reported results from individual studies included ergonomic assessment accuracies exceeding 95%, fatigue reductions of more than 50% in selected applications, and cycle-time reductions of up to 28.4%, along with improvements in task allocation, workload monitoring, and production efficiency. These values should not be interpreted as overall effects of Industry 5.0 technologies, given the heterogeneity of technologies, experimental designs, and assessment methods. Discussion The evidence was limited by laboratory validation, a lack of longitudinal research, heterogeneous assessment methods, and insufficient real-world implementation in specific industrial sectors.

documents.abstract: Industry 5.0 (I5.0) emphasizes industrial technologies that are human-centric, sustainable, and resilient. Human-Centric Digital Twins (HCDTs) support this transition by integrating worker data with robots, machines, tasks, and industrial environments. However, the relevant research remains fragmented across human modelling, Human–Robot Collaboration, Artificial Intelligence (AI), simulation, and Digital Twin (DT) research. Moreover, systems that use human data or adaptive automation are often described as human-centric without demonstrating measurable benefits to workers. This review addresses these limitations by distinguishing HCDTs from conventional human models, Human DTs, and collaborative robotic systems. It critically examines human-focused sensing, multi-modal data integration, biomechanical modelling, intention and motion prediction, robotic simulation, optimization, reinforcement learning, immersive interfaces, industrial connectivity, and data governance. Based on this analysis, a literature-derived conceptual framework is proposed that connects sensing, integration, human modelling, analytics, simulation, decision-making, adaptation, human interaction, and governance. The framework organizes the functional requirements of HCDTs and is intended to inform future system design and comparison; its practical applicability and effectiveness require further validation. The review argues that HCDTs must extend beyond worker monitoring and productivity maximization: human data should inform industrial decisions that produce measurable improvements in safety, ergonomics, wellbeing, autonomy, accessibility, or skill development. Such systems should also uphold privacy, transparency, uncertainty awareness, explainability, and appropriate human authority. By linking technological capabilities to explicit worker outcomes, this synthesis enables researchers and engineers to assess the human-centeredness of HCDT implementations and supports the development of trustworthy systems for I5.0.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in land governance, reshaping how environmental pressures and sustainability goals are addressed. Yet the institutional processes through which human–AI collaboration takes shape remain largely unexplored. This study examines whether human–AI collaboration is emerging as a new governance paradigm in China’s land sector, and if so, through what institutional pathways and practical forms it is being articulated and implemented. Drawing on a systematic analysis of 352 policy documents and case studies from coastal regions, the study develops and applies the CTI framework—an analytical lens that integrates Contextual conditions, Technological capabilities, and Institutional arrangements. The findings reveal three interrelated developments: (1) policy discourse constructs a coherent narrative in which environmental pressures and digital transformation jointly create an imperative for change; (2) a systematic division of labor between AI and human officials emerges in policy and is reflected in practice, with AI handling data processing and preliminary screening while humans retain final decision-making, value judgment, and accountability; and (3) this division is being institutionalized through a staged process of policy guidance, pilot mechanisms, and institutional adaptation. These developments suggest that human–AI collaboration may be taking shape as an emerging governance paradigm in land governance, one that is beginning to be codified and tested in policy and practice. The study contributes an integrative analytical framework, specifies the logic of human–machine division of labor, and extends collaborative governance theory beyond its traditional human-centric assumptions. The findings also carry implications for governance contexts where human–AI collaboration is reshaping land governance and other policy domains.

documents.abstract: Abstract This research involved co-creating a systematic review analysis alongside the world’s smartest humanoid robot, Ami. The work involved a human-humanoid collaboration in understanding driving under the influence of drugs’ (DUIDs’) prevalence, implications and chemical analysis. The systematic review was conducted according to the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis guidelines. Quantitative studies reporting drugs encountered in DUID published between 2007 – 2025 were included. Studies that had no confirmatory chemical analysis were excluded. Included studies ( n = 25) were analysed independently by researchers and integrated into Ami’s knowledge-based system. Ami deployed large language models for analysis but often needed prompt to extract information. The results showed similarity in extraction between the systematic review and the humanoid analysis. Both approaches confirmed key drugs reported in DUID were alcohol, cannabinoids, cocaine, amphetamine, benzodiazepines, and opiates. Such drugs were often detected in blood and urine and less occasionally in oral fluid. Key techniques employed for their analysis were immunoassay, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, where the latter was the most sensitive technique. Implications of these drugs on driving included impairment, increased risk of accidents, with fatal accidents less frequent but more severe. No AI hallucinations were encountered in Ami’s answers; yet, examples were used from outside the studies integrated into the knowledge-based system. This showed that the humanoid is integrating experience and knowledge from other sourcing and adapting them in the present study. In summary, the humanoid offered a valuable and quick tool in analysis and can support healthcare research.

As the dimensionality and complexity of engineering data grows, traditional machine learning systems become increasinglydifficult to apply, especially when detecting informative features without sacrificing predictive accuracy and computationalefficiency. In this paper we proposed a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning Framework for Intelligent Feature Optimization andPredictive Analytics in Engineering Applications. The framework is a combination of classical data preprocessing, intelligentfeature selection, quantum-enhanced feature representation, parameterized quantum circuits and predictive learning in a unifiedoptimization pipeline. Engineering features are first normalized and evaluated to find informative subsets and minimizeredundancy. These selected features are then mapped onto the quantum feature space and parameterized quantum circuits tocreate improved representations for predictive modeling. The optimization objective takes into account predictive loss, size ofthe feature subset and regularization to achieve an efficient feature configuration. This quantum-classical representation is fed to the classical predictive models for classification and evaluation of the models. The framework is assessed based on predictiveaccuracy, ROC properties, feature reduction, convergence behavior, computational time, scalability and prediction error. Thepotential of using intelligent feature optimization combined with quantum enhanced representation for engineering analytics isillustrated by comparing it to conventional machine learning and hybrid learning models. This study provides a flexibleframework that enables the merging of quantum and classic machine learning, and shows how hybrid architectures can be usedin high-dimensional engineering prediction.

Abstract Hybrid approaches can help organizational actors learn and adjust to feedback. This chapter explores the knowledge-based view of organizations, which describes how organizations integrate knowledge from internal and external actors and rely on both explicit and tacit knowledge. Hybrid organizing enables organizational learning and innovation by integrating diverse logics and perspectives. Social impact organizers can cultivate hybrid synergy and productive tension by adopting mindset-shaping strategies that recognize both contradiction and complementarity. Examples from research and real life show how social impact organizers use hybridity to adapt and survive in turbulent environments and suggest an emerging area of research in human–artificial intelligence partnerships for social impact organizing.

When a SCADA alarm is raised in a water distribution network, operators must decide quickly whether it reflects a cyberattack, a physical fault, a normal transient or a faulty sensor. Supervised classifiers need labelled incidents that utilities rarely have, and frontier large language models (LLMs) take tens of seconds per decision. We tested whether Jev, a training-free model that returns class probabilities in about one second, can serve as the first tier of this triage. On a four-class cause-attribution benchmark built on the C-Town network in EPANET, Jev was compared with a hand-written rule tree, a supervised classifier and seven cloud LLMs on identical evidence in four sealed, pre-registered rounds. With only a label-free prior correction, Jev matched the rule tree (macro-F1 0.62-0.64 against 0.56-0.61 in distribution) and exceeded the supervised classifier by 0.36-0.42 on event subtypes absent from its labels, in all four rounds, and it outperformed the classifier whenever fewer than about four labelled events per class were available. Jev also decided 20-40 times faster than frontier LLMs. Accepting only benign Jev verdicts confirmed by the rule tree spared an LLM reviewer 35-38% of windows on fresh sealed sets without loss of macro-F1. Transferred unchanged to two further networks, this gated cascade stayed within the non-inferiority margin of its reviewer on all four sets. A fast, training-free screen can therefore take over about a third of the review load in SCADA anomaly triage while preserving the accuracy of deliberate review.

Abstract Cognitive load assessment using functional nearinfrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has gained increasing attention due to its non-invasive and high spatial resolution nature. However, reliable classification remains challenging due to non-stationary and nonlinear nature of haemodynamic signals. Conventional time-frequency representation methods often fails to capture subtle amplitude variations from haemodynamic responses due to limited joint time-frequency resolutions. In this study, an attempt has been made to characterize and estimate cognitive load using single-channel fNIRS and Hyperlet Transform (HLT). The framework integrates preprocessing, HLT based time-frequency decomposition, multidomain feature extraction, and optimal feature selection within a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) folds to identify robust biomarkers. The extracted features are applied to five ML classifiers namely SVM-RBF, KNN, Naive Bayes, AdaBoost, and Random Forest. Among the evaluated classifiers, Support Vector Machine with a Radial Basis Function kernel achieved highest performance with an accuracy of 73.33% for 3-class tasks, followed by 86.67% and 90.00% for Baseline vs Low and Baseline vs High Cognitive Load tasks. Further, HLT outperformed conventional time-frequency methods, which emphasizes that HLT derived features effectively capture cognitive workload related hemodynamic changes and provides strong potential for development of real-time deployable solutions for next-generation affective computing systems.

Background: Brain tumor surgery aims to achieve maximal safe resection while preserving neurological function; however, accurate intraoperative discrimination between tumor tissue and normal brain remains a major challenge. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) has emerged as a promising label-free optical imaging modality that provides quantitative information on tissue biochemical and physiological characteristics. The integration of machine learning (ML) has further enhanced its potential for automated tissue classification and real-time intraoperative decision support. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence regarding HSI and ML in brain tumor surgery, highlighting technological principles, clinical applications, current limitations, and future directions. Methods: This narrative review was based on a comprehensive literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify studies evaluating the application of HSI and artificial intelligence (AI) in brain tumor surgery. The search strategy included combinations of the keywords “ hyperspectral imaging ,” “ brain tumor ,” “ glioma ,” “ machine learning ,” “ deep learning ,” “ artificial intelligence ,” and “ neurosurgery .” Priority was given to peer-reviewed original research articles, narrative and systematic reviews, and clinically relevant investigations describing the technical development, intraoperative application, and translational potential of HSI in neurooncology. Landmark studies that established the foundations of HSI, together with recent publications reflecting advances in ML and clinical implementation, were preferentially included to provide both historical context and contemporary perspectives. Manual screening of the reference lists of key publications was performed to identify additional relevant studies. As a narrative review, this manuscript was intended to provide a critical overview of current evidence rather than a systematic assessment of the literature. Consequently, no formal study selection algorithm, quality assessment tool, or quantitative meta-analysis was performed. Results: Current evidence indicates that HSI combined with ML enables accurate intraoperative tissue classification, improved tumor margin delineation, and emerging molecular characterization, including prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation status. Deep learning approaches generally outperform conventional ML techniques by integrating spectral and spatial information. Although early clinical studies have demonstrated encouraging diagnostic performance, widespread implementation remains limited by heterogeneous imaging protocols, relatively small patient cohorts, limited multicenter validation, and computational challenges. Conclusion: HSI represents a promising adjunct for precision-guided brain tumor surgery by providing real-time biochemical tissue characterization without the need for exogenous contrast agents. Continued advances in AI, standardized imaging protocols, multicenter clinical validation, and multimodal intraoperative integration will be essential to facilitate routine clinical adoption and establish its impact on surgical and patient outcomes.

Developing cognitive models of algorithmic reasoning from behavioral data is a central problem in cognitive science that challenges current methods. Traditional approaches to cognitive modeling are interpretable and benefit from human expertise, but lack flexibility and scalability. Emerging techniques using large language models (LLMs) for de novo generation of cognitive models are scalable and flexible, but lack a role for human expertise and have mostly been applied to simpler tasks than algorithm recovery. We propose a hybrid system that treats discovery of cognitive algorithms as a program refinement problem. Human-created cognitive models are expressed as probabilistic programs and provided to a system of LLM agents with a mandate to: identify mismatches between model and behavior; propose code-level modifications within researcher-specified constraints; and verify structural fidelity. Revisions propagate to a probabilistic inference module that performs inference for latent variables and data likelihood computations. We evaluate the pipeline on human behavior in a problem-solving paradigm that exposes a variety of cognitive algorithms. Revised models consistently improve model fit relative to ancestral models and reveal a small set of recurring innovations that capture meaningful behavioral variability in this task.

I·V·O Lens Prompt v4.1 is the current canonical reference version of the I·V·O Lens, a domain-independent framework for structural analysis using: O — Structured PossibilityV — Instantiated RelationI — Situated Selectivity Version 4.1 retains the operator semantics frozen in v4.0 and introduces additional epistemic safeguards developed from reproducible cross-model failure modes. The v4.1 safeguards strengthen: evidence provenance and claim-status separation; distinction between observation, event, class, membership and mechanism; separation of hypothesized mechanisms from established structural conditions; treatment of UNRESOLVED versus supported negative claims; evidential dependency and uncertainty propagation; causal-status calibration; requirements for assigning Situated Selectivity (I); synthesis and intervention constraints. The release candidate underlying v4.1 was frozen and tested in a controlled cross-model Hessdalen regression using Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. The regression substantially reduced the targeted failure modes without collapsing the analysis into blanket uncertainty. The exact tested RC2 artefact is retained in the release archive for reproducibility. Data and code for a systematic review of the urban climate literature. A large language model extracted structured information from the full text of every paper, and domain experts checked a sample of that extraction. This package lets you check the data and rebuild the paper's statistics, tables and figures. Start here Read README.md first. make check checks your setup. uv sync --extra dev installs the pinned environment, make paper-all rebuilds the statistics and tables, make figures draws the figures, and make ci-test runs the tests. No API keys are needed. data/README.md explains which values came from the model, which from fixed code, and which from the experts. Contents data/extracted_metadata/: 9,284 records, one per paper, as the model extracted them data/enrichments/ and data/contribution_rationales/: 9,284 records each of values computed from the extraction, and the reasoning behind each contribution label data/volunteer_review/: the anonymized expert review responses from both validation rounds, and the record of how a third reviewer settled the disagreements in the blind second round data/cross_model_validation/: comparisons with other models that support the choice of extraction model data/experiments/recall_audit_2025/: the search-recall audit, with its query strings, per-journal counts and the screening decision for each extra paper, and the check of how papers were assigned to publication years, with the corrected annual series data/contribution_reproducibility/: the earlier contribution labels the revision table is checked against, and the contribution classifier's attestation and the production promotion manifest that binds it src/, tests/, Makefile and uv.lock: the analysis code and its tests License Everything in this deposit, data and code alike, is released under CC-BY-4.0. This version Final archive for the accepted manuscript. Compared with version 4.0 (23 September 2026), the extracted records and the set of papers are unchanged. Each paper's world region and income group are now joined on ISO 3166 country codes rather than on country names, which fills them in for 236 records whose country names had not matched (mostly studies in Turkey, Taiwan and the Netherlands); country names in the enrichment records follow ISO 3166, and figures and tables use short names such as Iran, South Korea and Vietnam. The method-combination figure now counts every combination, including machine-learning models used alone.

The digital revolution is transforming modern education as it moves from teacher lecture to learner-centered, interactive methods. Immersive technologies augment learning using Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Extended Reality (XR) in conjunction with the use of multimedia to enable experiential and collaborative learning. This chapter gives a review of concepts, pedagogical foundations, applications and implementation of immersive technology in various educational fields. It also explores the effectiveness of learning, the implementation challenges, ethical issues, and future trends like Metaverse education, adaptive XR and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Moreover, the chapter reviews the recent literature and outlines the gaps in the current research to offer practical implications for the educators, instructional designers, and researchers.

Background Osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous whole-joint disorder influenced by mechanical stress, aging, previous trauma, genetic susceptibility, subchonrral bone alterations, and localized inflamation.Emerging evidence suggests that immune and metabolic processes alterations may be involved in OA pathogenesis particularly in inflammatory and metabolically dysregulated subtypes. Content This narrative review summarizes the bidirectional crosstalk between immune and metabolic processes during OA progression. Human observational studies and experimental models suggest that immune-cell activation and metabolic dysfunction may interact to influence synovial inflammation and cartilage homeostasis although their causal relevance and relative contributions vary across OA phenotypes. We further discuss emerging immunometabolic strategies targeting glycolytic and lipid-metabolic pathways as well as predominantly experimental approaches involving gene editing synthetic biology and stem cell-based therapies. Conclusion Integrating multi-omics technologies with personalized medicine may improve patient stratification and dynamic monitoring and could facilitate the future development of more personalized and potentially disease-modifying strategies for OA.Future research should focus on clarifying the dynamic immunometabolic network underlying OA and promoting the clinical translation of innovative strategies through artificial intelligence and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Developing English language skills in ESL learners is a long-experienced challenge for teachers and the learners. In this scenario, consistent interaction with artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of orchestrating authentic interactions with the language is found to be useful in facilitating learners to acquire and master of English language skills. Such tools have the potential to create opportunities for learners to achieve personalised and interactive learning experiences, enable teachers to provide individualised feedback, and open avant-garde adaptive pathways for learning. Additionally, they may promote learners’ motivation, encourage their active participation, and engage them in self-directed learning procedures. Therefore, this exploratory single-participant case study aims to investigate whether exposure to AI has a positive impact on developing English language skills. The data were collected using a qualitative case study focused on an academic in a public university in Sri Lanka. The data collection methods included semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and observations. The results obtained during the action research and empirical study indicated that consistent interaction with AI tools facilitates the acquisition of English language skills and enables individuals to use them confidently in authentic situations.

Human resource management (HRM) is being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI). Organisations increasingly use AI to screen applicants, schedule interviews, personalise learning, provide continuous performance feedback, predict attrition, answer employee queries and allocate work. These AI-enabled HR practices promise efficiency, consistency and personalisation, but they also alter the relationship between employees and the organisation in ways that shape attitudes, behaviours and performance. This chapter examines the impact of AI-enabled HR practices on organisational behaviour and employee performance. It first clarifies the concepts of electronic HRM, HR analytics, algorithmic HRM and AI-enabled HRM and traces their evolution. It then reviews AI applications across the HR value chain, from workforce planning and recruitment to learning, performance management, compensation, engagement, retention and HR service delivery. Drawing on the ability–motivation–opportunity framework, social exchange theory, organisational justice theory, the job demands–resources model, psychological contract theory and technology acceptance theories, the chapter explains the mechanisms through which AI-enabled HR practices influence trust, perceived fairness, engagement, job satisfaction, autonomy, technostress, job insecurity and, ultimately, task, contextual and innovative performance. A synthesis of empirical evidence shows that effects are contingent: AI-enabled HR practices tend to improve outcomes when they are transparent, fair, augmentative and supported by leadership, and to undermine them when they are opaque, controlling or perceived as reductive. The chapter proposes an integrative conceptual framework with research propositions, discusses ethical and legal considerations, including India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and offers practical guidance for managers.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Astronomy and space are undergoing a transformation in how they are explored and understood by human visitors, thanks to technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), satellite imaging, mobile applications, smart telescopes, and astrophotography devices. Mobile Sky Mapping Applications allow visitors to find planets, stars, and constellations in real time. Weather predictions, visibility updates, and customized tips for optimal viewing conditions are all possible with AI systems. Similarly, AR and VR technologies can offer a virtual experience by generating simulated space and astronomical phenomena, enabling tourists to virtually travel through space to explore galaxies and planets that would be impossible to reach in the real world. Telescopes have become more accessible to amateur astronomers and tourists, thanks to new telescope technology and automated observatories. Satellite technology is utilized to help determine areas with dark skies and reduced light pollution. These technologies enhance tourists’ engagement and learning, raise scientific awareness, help protect the environment, and boost economic opportunities for tourism areas in remote regions. The results of this study point to the potential of different technologies to transform astro tourism and offer new, educational, and immersive experiences worldwide.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly available to students, but their educational value depends on how they are configured, constrained, and integrated into course practices. This technology report describes a no-code workflow for implementing a course-specific chatbot in upper-division undergraduate biochemistry using a custom GPT configured with instructor-generated lecture slides, class transcripts, handouts, syllabus information, and custom instructions. The workflow emphasized course alignment, frequent updating, instructor validation, assessment scoping, and student prompt guidance. The chatbot was used in biochemistry I lecture across two consecutive fall offerings and extended to biochemistry II lecture for follow-up use. Student survey responses indicated substantial adoption and generally positive perceptions; peer-led supplemental instruction attendance and course-grade data are presented only as contextual information. The report highlights a practical, transferable approach for using no-code custom GPT tools to extend course-aligned study support while preserving instructor oversight and existing academic support structures.

documents.abstract: Uzbekistan has moved further and faster on small-business reform than most countries in the post-Soviet region. Between 2017 and 2025 the share of small business in GDP rose from roughly one third to over half, and the number of registered small entities reached 1.21 million by October 2025 (State Statistics Agency, 2025). The country was recognised as one of the five largest global improvers in the 2024 Women, Business and the Law index, with an 11.9-point gain taking its score to 82.5 (World Bank, 2024). The Uzbekistan-2030 strategy targets a doubling of exports and an increase in the number of exporting enterprises from roughly 5,700 to 15,000 (Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, 2024).These figures have been read almost exclusively through an economic and engineering lens. The dominant policy frame treats market infrastructure as a matter of roads, customs procedures, payment systems, credit lines and digital platforms. That frame is not wrong. It is incomplete in a specific and consequential way, and the way it is incomplete is sociological. This article makes a conceptual argument rather than reporting new data. Our contribution is not the observation that markets are socially embedded, which has been established since Polanyi (1944) and Granovetter (1985). It is threefold and more specific.First, we argue that the social layer of market infrastructure should be treated as infrastructure in its own right, not as context surrounding the "real" infrastructure. This extends to a post-Soviet setting the argument developed by Elyachar (2010) for Cairo, where the communicative channels produced by women's everyday sociality function as economic infrastructure in the same register as roads and telephone lines, and it connects that argument to Star's (1999) and Larkin's (2013) insistence that infrastructure is relational and becomes visible only through the practices that sustain or fail to sustain it.Second, we specify the mechanism by which social structure acts on formally universal infrastructure. We call it differential access filtering, and we decompose it using the four sources of social capital distinguished by Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993), namely value introjection, bounded solidarity, reciprocity exchanges and enforceable trust. Two of these enable market participation and two constrain it, which gives the framework an internal reason to expect both positive and negative effects rather than asserting one or the other.Third, we propose Uzbekistan as a scope condition for embeddedness theory. Most of the informality and embeddedness literature has examined settings where formal institutions were weak, absent or decaying (Mair and Martí, 2009;Williams and Shahid, 2016). Uzbekistan presents the inverse configuration, in which formal market infrastructure is being built rapidly and from above onto a dense, legally codified communal institution. The theoretical question this raises is whether embeddedness under rapid state-led formalisation produces bridging or closure, and our answer is that it systematically produces both, with the balance determined by which of the four mechanisms a given reform activates.The article proceeds as follows. Section 2 develops the theoretical framing. Section 3 sets out the fivelayer framework and its social mediators. Section 4 reads the mahalla symmetrically. Section 5 applies the framework differentially to five entrepreneurial positions. Section 6 states explicitly what the available evidence does and does not support. Section 7 discusses feasibility of the policy implications. Section 8 sets out the theoretical contribution, limitations, testable propositions and research agenda.Infrastructure studies in sociology and anthropology have moved decisively away from treating infrastructure as a stock of physical assets. Star (1999) argued that infrastructure is relational rather than substantive, that it is embedded in other structures and practices, and that its distributional properties become visible mainly at the point of breakdown. Larkin (2013) extended this by treating infrastructures as objects that carry political and aesthetic meaning as well as goods, and by showing that the promise attached to an infrastructure is part of what it does. Graham and Marvin (2001) documented the process by which networked infrastructure, far from producing uniform access, splinters into premium and residual circuits. Elyachar (2010) took the argument one step further in a way that is directly relevant here. Studying microfinance and empowerment projects in Cairo, she showed that the communicative channels generated by women's routine sociality constitute a social infrastructure that carries economic traffic as surely as a road does, and that development interventions make this infrastructure visible precisely by attempting to capture or format it. We take this as our starting point. If social ties are infrastructure, then a five-layer account of market infrastructure is not a four-layer account plus context. It is an account of five infrastructures, one of which happens to be made of relationships.Economic sociology supplies the mechanism. Granovetter (1985) established that economic action is embedded in concrete networks of relations. Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993) then did the analytical work that the embeddedness literature most often omits, distinguishing four mechanisms by which social structure shapes economic action and, crucially, identifying their positive and negative consequences together. Value introjection and bounded solidarity generate commitment and mutual support but also generate demands for conformity. Reciprocity exchanges and enforceable trust lower transaction costs but also impose obligations that can drain the successful and restrict the individual autonomy on which enterprise growth depends. Portes and Landolt (1996) and Portes (1998) developed the resulting downsides, namely exclusion of outsiders, excess claims on group members, restrictions on individual freedom and downward levelling norms. We adopt this four-mechanism decomposition as the analytical core of our framework, because it is what allows a symmetrical reading of communal institutions rather than a celebratory one.Two further strands complete the framing. The contextualisation programme in entrepreneurship research insists that where and when entrepreneurship happens is constitutive rather than incidental (Welter, 2011;Welter et al., 2019), and Kloosterman's (2010) mixed embeddedness perspective shows how the resources an entrepreneur can mobilise from social networks interact with the opportunity structure that markets and regulation supply. Meanwhile, the entrepreneurial ecosystem literature has become the dominant policy vocabulary for the phenomena we describe, and its own systematic reviews concede that it remains largely atheoretical and built on advanced-economy assumptions, with resource scarcity, structural gaps and institutional voids distinguishing emergingeconomy ecosystems (Cao and Shi, 2021;Wurth et al., 2022). Our framework is intended in part as a sociological supplement to that literature, replacing its metaphor of an ecosystem of actors with an account of layered infrastructures and the filters that regulate access to them.By market infrastructure we mean the bundle of arrangements that allow a small firm to find customers, set prices, secure finance, manage logistics and enforce rights. We distinguish five layers. The physical layer covers roads, warehouses, bazaars and border posts. The financial layer covers banks, microfinance, payment instruments and credit lines. The digital layer covers e-commerce, platform identifiers, e-government and data systems (Nambisan, 2017;Bonina et al., 2021). The institutional layer covers registration, taxation, standards and dispute resolution. The social layer covers trust networks, reputational systems, professional associations, rotating savings groups and the mahalla.The analytically important claim is not the existence of five layers but the relation between them. Access to any of the first four layers is mediated through the fifth, and the fifth distributes that access unequally. A credit assessment reads a reputation that is produced in a network. A customs procedure is navigated with the help of brokers and peers who have navigated it before. A digital marketplace is adopted first by entrepreneurs whose existing ties already include early users, which is why platform adoption tends to follow pre-existing network structure rather than to disrupt it (Bonina et al., 2021).Where public investment addresses the first four layers without engaging the fifth, returns are eroded by filtering rather than by underprovision. The new road serves the bazaar of the better connected. The new credit line reaches firms with formal collateral. The new platform recruits younger urban men with smartphones and foreign-language skills. This is the splintering dynamic that Graham and Marvin (2001) described, produced here by social rather than commercial sorting.Urban evidence from Uzbekistan supports this reading at the level of the layers themselves. Farmanov et al. (2025), examining smart-city implementation in Bukhara, find that deployment of sensors, platforms and digital governance tools has run ahead of the inclusivity and citizen-engagement components, so that a technically advancing infrastructure is not correspondingly more usable. Dushanova et al. (2025) document the same asymmetry in the city's tourism infrastructure, where heritage sites, transport and wayfinding remain inaccessible to people with mobility impairments despite a national policy commitment to barrier-free provision. Both cases show a filter that is not social in the network sense but produces the same result, namely infrastructure that is formally universal and practically selective. They also support treating market infrastructure as a sociotechnical assembly rather than a technical one, which is the premise of Section 2.In the Uzbek case we identify five social mediators through which the filtering runs, namely mahalla networks, gender norms and the unpaid care burden, the urban-rural divide, the informal economy, and labour migration. These are not causes in a statistical sense and we do not claim to have estimated their effects. They are the channels through which formally universal infrastructure becomes differentially accessible, and Section 6 states precisely how much evidence stands behind each.Figure 1. Five-layer framework of market infrastructure for small entrepreneurship in Uzbekistan. Infrastructure layers reach policy outcomes only through social mediators. Each mediator has an enabling and a restricting side, corresponding to the four mechanisms of social capital in Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993). Which side dominates depends on the mechanism a given reform activates.mahalla solidarity has historically rested on residence rather than kinship or ethnicity, which gave it an unusually broad reach across social groups. Urinboyev and Eraliev (2022) describe the mahalla as a legally plural arena in which competing orders coexist and produce new organisational forms, some of them generative.On the restricting side, the record is at least as substantial and considerably older than our earlier draft acknowledged. Three findings matter for market infrastructure specifically.First, the mahalla's incorporation into public administration has converted an association of residents into an instrument of state administration and, in the assessment of a large body of work, of social control (Urinboyev, 2011;Noori, 2006;Human Rights Watch, 2003). Urinboyev and Eraliev (2022) situate this within broader debates on how non-democratic states neutralise civil-society institutions through administrative and legal incorporation. An entrepreneur's relationship with the mahalla is therefore not a purely horizontal relationship among peers. It carries a vertical dimension, and any policy that routes market infrastructure through the mahalla routes it through that vertical dimension too.Second, mahalla-based discretionary allocation has documented exclusionary effects along gender lines. Kamp (2004) shows that the delegation of welfare targeting to mahalla committees, staffed by untrained neighbours exercising discretion, placed divorced and abandoned women at particular risk of exclusion, and that solidarity among women in a mahalla cannot be assumed. This is bounded solidarity and enforceable trust operating exactly as Portes and Sensenbrenner predicted, producing support for insiders and exclusion at the boundary. If discretionary neighbourhood assessment produces this pattern in welfare, there is no principled reason to expect a different pattern when the same bodies certify cooperatives, endorse borrowers or vouch for exporters.Third, the conformity costs fall unevenly. Restrictions on individual autonomy and downward levelling norms are the two downsides of social capital most directly relevant to enterprise growth (Portes, 1998;Portes and Landolt, 1996). Ethnographic work on women traders in Uzbek bazaars describes exactly this tension, with women negotiating and renegotiating patriarchal norms rather than simply being enabled or simply being blocked by them (Kandiyoti, 2007).The implication for policy is that "recognise the mahalla" is an underspecified instruction. What matters is which mechanism a given reform activates. Instruments that work through reciprocity exchange, such as linking gap groups to formal microfinance, plausibly extend access. Instruments that work through discretionary gatekeeping, such as making mahalla endorsement a condition of registration, credit or certification, plausibly reproduce existing exclusions and add a vertical dependency. We return to this distinction in Section 7.A framework that applies identically to everyone explains nothing about distribution. Table 1 applies the five layers and their filters to five entrepreneurial positions whose constraints differ, which also responds to the reasonable objection that "small entrepreneurship" is not a single category. Three points follow from the table. The binding constraint differs by position, so a single infrastructure package cannot be expected to have uniform effects. The same mechanism that helps one position hinders another, which is why a framework built on Portes and Sensenbrenner's symmetric account is more useful here than one built on social capital as an unambiguous good. And the reforms most likely to backfire are, in several rows, the reforms currently most favoured, namely discretionary community endorsement and platform-first digitalisation.Two of the three policy outcomes named in the title deserve explicit grounding, since the framework is meant to bear on them.Export concentration is documented. In 2024 gold, services and industrial goods together accounted for roughly 70 percent of total exports (Observatory of Economic Complexity, 2025; U.S. Department of Commerce, 2025), and the number of exporting enterprises stood at around 5,700 in mid-2024 against the 2030 target of 15,000 (Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, 2024). The shortfall is usually read as a logistics and certification problem. Our framework suggests it is also a trust problem, since enforceable trust built on personal relationship and cash does not travel across borders and infrastructure that supplies no substitute concentrates gains among firms already connected to international buyers. The concentration is a fact; its attribution to social filtering is our proposition.Employment is where the filters compound. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Recent work introduces search into RLVR rollouts to increase trajectory diversity, but diversity alone does not ensure that the search-induced rollout policy improves upon the current policy. To address this gap, we propose APIVIS, a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning. APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It further applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens, preserving a learning signal when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. We show that exact value-guided selection improves the expected verifier reward at each searched state and that this guarantee extends to the complete rollout policy, with a corresponding approximate guarantee under bounded value-estimation error. Experiments on widely recognized mathematical reasoning benchmarks and different model scales demonstrate substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods, validating the effectiveness of APIVIS.

The increasing datafication of work has become a pervasive theme within organizations, particularly with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies that rely on data and machine learning to generate insights and decisions. Prior research has shown that datafication practices aimed at administrative control and accountability can transform organizations in profound and often unintended ways. Our research moves beyond investigating datafication for administrative purposes to explore how it unfolds when actors intend to extract knowledge through AI predictive modeling. Drawing on a three-year ethnography of a human resources (HR) department introducing AI for candidate screening, we find that datafication expanded far beyond the technology’s initially envisioned scope. We explain this scope expansion by introducing the concept of epistemic enchantment : a collective process through which organizational members become captivated and mobilized by AI’s promise to generate predictive, objective, and continuously improving insights from data, while overlooking the costs and risks involved. Our study reveals how datafication practices can expand endlessly as organizational members, enchanted by AI’s epistemic promises, pursue the notion of ideal data as an ever-desired but never reachable goal.

documents.abstract: The goal of program synthesis is to enable non-expert users to write programs by providing a specification instead of an implementation. To truly realize this goal, the specification must require no expertise and no effort to generate. We consider the problem of synthesizing automation scripts from only the logs that are automatically collected by many systems. Using our approach, users can automate tasks they usually perform manually, without having to know how to program them. Because logs are collected automatically, the synthesis approach needs to scale to large sets of logs. We present a new algorithm to solve this task by incrementally extending an API-calling script with behavior exemplified by a sequence of log events, adding one sequence at a time. By minimizing the program modifications at each step, we preserve user intent and synthesize a program as general as possible. We show that our approach, implemented in a tool LogLoom, scales to synthesis tasks with more traces and more complex programs than existing techniques. LogLoom synthesizes scripts that are identical to reference solutions for 60 out of 72 benchmarks, compared to 14 for an existing symbolic approach and 39 for an LLM.

Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from large language models coordinate specialized agents to tackle complex tasks, but effective workflows are difficult to design in advance. Test-time evolution refines workflows using execution feedback, yet broad revisions can disturb useful components, while re-executing unchanged requests can incur redundant computation. Inspired by the interplay of inheritance and selection in biological evolution, we introduce Inherit-MAS, which makes inheritance explicit at the workflow and execution levels. A meta-model first synthesizes a workflow of worker agents with declared roles, communication inputs, and tool permissions, and a separately prompted judge scores each executed candidate and diagnoses its deficiencies. In ordinary refinement rounds, \emph{workflow inheritance} starts from the latest completed candidate, may discard removable nodes judged unhelpful, and applies a validated edit to address the diagnosed deficiency. When the new candidate executes, \emph{execution inheritance} inherits eligible stored results only if the complete resolved request and execution context match, avoiding redundant model and tool calls. With GPT-4o-mini workers, Inherit-MAS achieves 55.4\% completion on WorkBench and 49.7\% joint F1 on HotpotQA FullWiki, outperforming EvoAgent, EvoMAS, and TacoMAS. With Qwen3-32B workers, it also exceeds these evolving-MAS baselines on both benchmarks. Compared with rerunning the same controller with execution inheritance disabled, execution inheritance reduces worker-token usage by 29.1\% on WorkBench and 34.6\% on HotpotQA, and total token usage by 5.3\% and 18.1\%.

In modern education, the information and communication technologies are having an increasing impact on personalized learning. Their implementation responds to the digital transformation in our society and requires the development of digital literacy as a key competence of both teachers and students. In Mathematics, Physics, Music and Art education, individualizing learning is supported by selected tools such as GeoGebra, Corinth 3D, Musescore, Solfy or graphic editors (GIMP, Procreate, Adobe Fresco). They enable adaptive and personalized forms of learning, support visualization, creativity, and self-directed learning. Although artificial intelligence presents challenges related to overreliance, academic integrity, and the development of critical and creative thinking, Information and communication technologies (ICT) and Artificial Intelligencie (AI) technologies can enhance education by supporting visualization, collaboration, creativity, differentiated instruction, and personalized learning.

The article is devoted to the analysis of the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on the structure of interaction and communication mechanisms in digital games. Against the background of the rapid development of generative technologies, video games are becoming media platforms in which AI not only provides personalization and scenario adaptation, but also forms new forms of role identity, cognitive engagement and political socialization. The research is based on an interdisciplinary approach combining media theoretical, political-analytical and critical-discursive analysis. Three game projects are considered as an empirical basis, in which AI acts as a media intermediary that sets the framework for the interpretation, control and representation of power. The comparative analysis makes it possible to identify the key functions of AI: from algorithmic selection of meanings to modeling digital subjectivity. It is concluded that AI in games functions as a political and communication actor that transforms the rules of interaction and the architecture of user experience.
